title: Number of Islands
statement: Given a 2D grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), count the islands. An island is land connected horizontally or vertically and surrounded by water.

nearMiss.why: A grid suggests a DP table, but connectivity isn't a recurrence over row and column prefixes.
Matrix-manipulation problems transform indices (rotate, spiral); this one explores connected regions.
There's no simultaneous spread to time; you flood one island at a time.

trigger.why: Connected regions in a grid ⇒ flood fill (DFS/BFS) from each unvisited land cell; each flood is one island.

ds.answer: The char[][] grid itself (mark visited by sinking to '0') or boolean[][] visited; recursion or ArrayDeque<int[]>
wrong: int[][] dp of island counts per prefix
ds.why: Marking visited in place keeps extra space to the recursion/queue.

invariant.answer: Every land cell reachable from an already-counted cell has been marked, so each new unvisited '1' starts a new island.
wrong: Each row contains at most one island.
Islands are counted when water is found.
A cell is marked only after all four neighbours are checked.
invariant.why: Each flood fill consumes exactly one connected component.

time.why: Each cell visited a constant number of times.

space.answer: O(rows × cols) worst case for the recursion stack or queue
space.why: A grid full of land makes the DFS stack (or BFS queue) large.

wrong: DP can't be used on grids.
DP would count water instead of land.
DP needs the grid to be square.

approach: For each cell == '1': count++, then DFS/BFS sinking all connected '1's to '0'.

twists.change: Land is added one cell at a time, and you report the island count after each addition.
twists.statement: A grid starts as all water. Positions are turned into land one at a time; after each addition, return the current number of islands (4-directionally connected land).
twists.ds: int[] parent over m · n cells with path compression, plus an island counter

nearMiss.why: A fresh flood fill after every addition is O(k · m · n); DSU merges incrementally.
There are no distances to compute; only components merging.
No in-place traversal trick tracks merging components.

twists.why: Online connectivity with only merges ⇒ union-find: each new land cell is +1 island, and each union with a land neighbour is −1.
twists.approach: On add (r, c): if already land, repeat the count; else count++, then for each land neighbour if union succeeds count−−. Record count.

title: Word Ladder
statement: Given beginWord, endWord and a word list, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in the list. Return 0 if impossible.

nearMiss.why: DFS over all sequences explores exponentially many paths and doesn't find the shortest first.
Edit distance compares two fixed strings; here you need a path through a dictionary.
Dijkstra is for weighted edges; every step costs 1, so plain BFS is shortest.

wrong: changing one letter at a time
every intermediate word must be in the list
trigger.why: Shortest number of equal-cost steps between states ⇒ BFS, generating neighbours by changing each letter.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<String> queue + HashSet<String> word set (remove words when visited)
ds.why: The set gives O(1) membership and doubles as the visited marker.

invariant.answer: Words are dequeued in order of their distance from beginWord, and each is enqueued at most once.
wrong: Every word in the list is enqueued at the start.
A word may be enqueued once per neighbour.
invariant.why: So the first time endWord is reached, its level is the shortest length.

time.answer: O(N · L · 26), N words of length L (×L more for building strings)
time.why: Each word generates L · 26 candidate neighbours.

space.why: The set and the queue hold words.

wrong: Backtracking needs the word list sorted.
Backtracking only works on words of length 3.

approach: BFS from beginWord, level by level. For each word, try every position × 'a'..'z'; if the candidate is in the set, remove it and enqueue. Return level + 1 when endWord appears.

twists.change: Each letter change has its own cost.
twists.statement: Transform beginWord into endWord by changing one letter at a time through dictionary words, where changing a letter to c costs cost[c]. Return the minimum total cost.
twists.ds: PriorityQueue<Object[]> of {cost, word} and HashMap<String, Integer> best

nearMiss.why: BFS minimises the number of steps, which is wrong once steps have different costs.
There's one source, and edges aren't unit-weight.
The word graph has cycles and no dependency order.

twists.why: Weighted edges, non-negative ⇒ Dijkstra over the word graph.
twists.approach: Dijkstra from beginWord; neighbours by changing each position to each letter (if in the dictionary) with weight cost[letter].

title: Clone Graph
statement: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph (possibly with cycles), return a deep copy of the graph. Each node has a value and a list of neighbours.

nearMiss.why: Tree recursion has no cycles; without a visited map, cloning a cyclic graph recurses forever.
Copy List with Random Pointer is similar, but each node here has many neighbours, not one next.
You need to copy structure, not merge components.

wrong: a deep copy of the graph
trigger.why: Traversal of a cyclic graph ⇒ DFS/BFS with a visited map; here the map is original → clone.

ds.answer: HashMap<Node, Node> original → clone, plus recursion or ArrayDeque<Node>
wrong: ArrayList<Node> of clones in input order
ds.why: The map is both the visited set and the lookup for already-made clones.

invariant.answer: A node's clone is put in the map BEFORE its neighbours are visited, so cycles find the existing clone.
wrong: Clones are created after all neighbours are cloned.
Each node is cloned once per incoming edge.
The map holds only leaf nodes.
invariant.why: Registering first is what stops infinite recursion.

time.why: Each node and edge once.

wrong: Tree DFS only works on binary trees with sorted keys.
Tree DFS would copy each node twice.

approach: clone(node): if in map return it; copy = new Node(val); map.put(node, copy); for each neighbour add clone(neighbour); return copy.

twists.change: The structure is a linked list with random pointers, and extra space must be O(1).
twists.statement: Each node of a linked list has a next pointer and a random pointer to any node or null. Deep-copy the list using O(1) extra space beyond the new nodes.
twists.trigger: using O(1) extra space beyond the new nodes
twists.ds: ListNode references: interleave copies (A → A' → B → B'), then split

nearMiss.why: Traversal with an old → new HashMap works but uses O(n) extra space.
The map is exactly the O(n) space you're not allowed.
There's no cycle or middle to find.

twists.why: Weave each copy right after its original so copy.random = original.random.next, then unweave.
twists.approach: Pass 1: insert copies after originals. Pass 2: set copy.random. Pass 3: restore originals' next and link the copies.

title: Rotting Oranges
statement: In a grid, 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange and 2 is a rotten orange. Every minute, fresh oranges next to a rotten one become rotten. Return the minimum minutes until no fresh orange remains, or −1 if impossible.

nearMiss.why: One BFS per rotten orange repeats work; all rotten oranges spread at the same time.
Spread happens in all directions at once; a row/column DP sweep doesn't model simultaneous time steps.
Connectivity says whether oranges are reachable, not how many minutes it takes.

trigger.answer: Every minute, fresh oranges next to a rotten one become rotten
trigger.why: Simultaneous spread from many sources, measured in time steps ⇒ multi-source BFS: all rotten cells start in the queue.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<int[]> seeded with every rotten cell + a fresh counter
wrong: boolean[][] visited with one BFS per source
int[][] dp filled row by row
ds.why: One queue, one BFS; the fresh count detects −1.

invariant.answer: After processing t layers, every orange within t steps of an initially rotten one is rotten.
wrong: Each layer contains exactly one orange.
The queue only ever holds the original rotten oranges.
Fresh oranges are enqueued at the start.
invariant.why: BFS layers = minutes.

wrong: O(k × rows × cols) for k rotten
time.why: Each cell enqueued at most once.

space.why: The queue in the worst case.

wrong: Plain BFS can't detect unreachable oranges.
BFS would need the grid sorted.

approach: Enqueue all 2s, count 1s. BFS layer by layer, rotting fresh neighbours and decrementing fresh; minutes++ per non-final layer. Return fresh == 0 ? minutes : −1.

twists.change: Each fresh orange takes its own number of minutes to rot once a neighbour is rotten.
twists.statement: In a grid of oranges, rot spreads from rotten oranges to adjacent fresh ones, but fresh orange (r, c) takes delay[r][c] minutes to rot once a neighbour has rotted. Return when the last orange rots, or -1.
twists.ds: PriorityQueue<int[]> of {time, r, c} seeded with every rotten orange

nearMiss.why: BFS levels assume every step takes one minute; with different delays a FIFO queue no longer pops in time order.
Plain flood fill ignores timing.
Rot spreads in all directions, so there's no fill order.

twists.why: Many sources + weighted steps ⇒ Dijkstra seeded with all sources.
twists.approach: Push all rotten at time 0; poll earliest; for a fresh neighbour, t = time + delay; relax if better. Answer = max time, or -1 if any fresh remains.

title: 01 Matrix
statement: Given a binary matrix, return a matrix where each cell holds the distance to the nearest 0 (moving up, down, left or right).

nearMiss.why: A BFS from every 1 to find its nearest 0 is O((rows · cols)²).
All steps cost 1, so Dijkstra's heap is unnecessary.
Components don't give distances.

trigger.why: Distance to the nearest of many sources ⇒ start BFS from all sources (every 0) at once.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<int[]> seeded with every 0 cell + int[][] dist initialised to −1 (unvisited)
wrong: boolean[][] visited with one BFS per 1
ds.why: One BFS fills every distance.

invariant.answer: Cells are dequeued in non-decreasing distance from the nearest 0, so a cell's first assigned distance is final.
wrong: Each cell's distance is updated many times.
Cells are processed row by row.
Only cells containing 1 are enqueued at the start.
invariant.why: Standard BFS ordering from a super-source.

time.why: Each cell once.

wrong: One BFS per cell is O(1) per cell anyway.
BFS needs the matrix to be square.

approach: Enqueue every 0 with dist 0; others −1. BFS: for each neighbour with dist −1, set dist = cur + 1 and enqueue. (Two DP sweeps also work.)

title: Course Schedule
statement: There are numCourses courses and a list of prerequisite pairs [a, b] meaning you must take b before a. Return true if it is possible to finish all courses.

nearMiss.why: Union-Find detects cycles in UNDIRECTED graphs; prerequisites are directed.
Plain DFS/BFS reachability doesn't detect a directed cycle unless you add in-progress state (which is topological sort).
Taking any available course first works only because of the topological order; the pattern is Kahn's algorithm.

trigger.answer: you must take b before a
trigger.why: Ordering constraints ⇒ directed graph; 'can everything finish?' ⇔ no directed cycle ⇔ a topological order exists.

ds.answer: List<List<Integer>> adjacency + int[] in-degree + ArrayDeque<Integer> queue
ds.why: Kahn's algorithm needs edges, in-degrees and a queue of ready nodes.

invariant.answer: A course enters the queue only when all its prerequisites have been taken.
wrong: Courses are taken in numeric order.
Every course starts in the queue.
A course is enqueued once per prerequisite.
invariant.why: If fewer than numCourses are ever taken, the rest sit on a cycle.

time.why: Each node and edge once.

wrong: Union-Find is too slow for 2000 courses.

approach: Build adjacency b → a and in-degrees. Queue all 0-in-degree courses; pop, count, decrement neighbours, enqueue new zeros. Return count == numCourses.

twists.change: Links between courses are undirected 'related' pairs, and you ask whether they contain a loop.
twists.statement: Courses are joined by undirected 'related to' pairs. Decide whether these links contain a cycle.

nearMiss.why: In-degrees only make sense with directed edges; on an undirected graph every edge counts both ways.
Distances don't matter.
There's nothing to choose; it's a connectivity check.

twists.why: Undirected cycle ⇒ an edge whose endpoints are already connected.
twists.approach: For each pair: if find(a) == find(b) return true; else union(a, b). Return false.

title: Course Schedule II
statement: Given numCourses and prerequisite pairs [a, b] (take b before a), return an order in which you can take all courses, or an empty array if that is impossible.

nearMiss.why: Sorting by some priority ignores the dependency edges.
Union-Find groups courses but can't order them, and misses directed cycles.
Trying permutations of courses is factorial.

trigger.answer: return an order in which you can take all courses
trigger.why: Produce an ordering consistent with 'before' constraints ⇒ topological sort.

ds.answer: Adjacency List<List<Integer>> + int[] in-degree + ArrayDeque<Integer>; output int[]
ds.why: Same as Course Schedule; record the pop order.

invariant.answer: The output so far lists courses whose prerequisites all appear earlier in it.
wrong: The output is sorted by course number.
Courses with more prerequisites appear first.
The output always contains numCourses entries.
invariant.why: If it ends short of numCourses, there is a cycle ⇒ return empty.

time.why: Kahn's algorithm.

wrong: A heap would need courses numbered from 1.
Heaps only work when there are no prerequisites.

approach: Kahn's algorithm; append each popped course to the order. Return the order if its size is numCourses, else an empty array.

title: Alien Dictionary
statement: You are given words from an alien language, sorted lexicographically by that language's unknown letter order. Derive an order of the letters consistent with the list, or return "" if the list is invalid.

nearMiss.why: A trie stores prefixes, but the letter order comes from the first differing character of adjacent words, i.e. edges in a graph.
Counting letters doesn't reveal their order.
You can't sort letters without first deriving the comparison rules.

trigger.answer: sorted lexicographically by that language's unknown letter order
wrong: return "" if the list is invalid
Derive an order of the letters
trigger.why: Adjacent sorted words give 'x before y' edges at their first difference; an order consistent with all edges ⇒ topological sort.

ds.answer: Map<Character, Set<Character>> edges + Map<Character, Integer> in-degree + ArrayDeque<Character>
ds.why: Sets avoid duplicate edges inflating in-degrees.

invariant.answer: Each pair of adjacent words contributes at most one edge: the first position where they differ.
wrong: Every pair of letters in a word creates an edge.
Letters in the first word come first.
Words are compared with every other word.
invariant.why: Only the first difference tells you anything; a longer word before its own prefix is invalid.

time.answer: O(C), C = total characters in all words
wrong: O(N²) comparisons of all word pairs
time.why: Adjacent comparisons plus a topological sort over ≤ 26 letters.

space.answer: O(1) for the graph (≤ 26 letters, ≤ 26² edges)

wrong: A trie needs the words unsorted.
Tries only work when all words are the same length.

approach: Add every letter as a node. For each adjacent pair, find the first differing char → edge (invalid if the longer word is a prefix and comes first). Kahn's algorithm; if not all letters are output, return "".

title: Accounts Merge
statement: Each account is a name followed by emails. Two accounts belong to the same person if they share any email. Merge the accounts so each person has one account with their emails sorted.

nearMiss.why: Grouping by name fails (different people can share a name), and pairwise email comparison is quadratic; you need transitive merging.
There are no ranges to sort and merge; 'merge' here means joining sets.
Emails aren't queried by prefix.

trigger.why: Sharing an element ⇒ same group, transitively ⇒ union-find (or connected components over emails).

ds.answer: Union-Find over emails (HashMap<String, String> parent) + HashMap<String, String> email → name
wrong: TreeMap<String, Integer> email → account index without merging
ds.why: Union each account's emails with its first email; then group by root.

invariant.answer: Two emails have the same root iff some chain of shared accounts connects them.
wrong: Each email's parent is the next email alphabetically.
Accounts with the same name are always unioned.
Every email is its own root at the end.
invariant.why: Grouping by find(email) yields each person's full set.

time.answer: O(E · α(E) + E log E), E = total emails
time.why: Near-constant unions/finds, plus sorting each group.

wrong: Hashing would sort the emails wrongly.
Hashing can't handle more than two accounts.

approach: For each account, union every email with its first email and record email → name. Group emails by find(email), sort each group, prefix the name.

title: Redundant Connection
statement: A tree of n nodes had one extra undirected edge added. Given the edges in order, return an edge that can be removed so the result is a tree; if several work, return the one that appears last in the input.

nearMiss.why: Topological sort detects cycles in DIRECTED graphs; these edges are undirected.
With the extra edge it's no longer a tree, so tree recursion would loop.
No local choice; you need to know when an edge first closes a cycle.

trigger.why: Process undirected edges in order; the first edge whose endpoints are already connected closes the cycle ⇒ union-find.

ds.answer: int[] parent and int[] rank (union-find)
ds.why: union returns false exactly when the edge is redundant.

invariant.answer: After processing edges 0..i, components reflect exactly those edges; an edge with both ends in one component closes a cycle.
wrong: Each node's parent is its smallest neighbour.
The number of components increases with each edge.
The redundant edge always touches node 1.
invariant.why: In a tree plus one edge, that edge is the only one that fails to merge.

time.why: One union/find per edge.

wrong: Topological sort can't handle more than n edges.
Topological sort needs node 1 to be the root.
Topological sort would remove the first edge instead of the last.

approach: For each edge (u, v): if find(u) == find(v) return it; else union(u, v).

title: Network Delay Time
statement: A network has n nodes and directed edges (u, v, w) where a signal takes w time to travel from u to v. A signal is sent from node k. Return the time until all nodes receive it, or −1 if some never do.

nearMiss.why: Plain BFS gives the fewest edges, not the least total time when edges have different weights.
Topological order needs a DAG and doesn't minimise weighted distance by itself.
There's a single source and weighted edges; layer counting doesn't apply.

wrong: A signal is sent from node k
trigger.why: Weighted (non-negative) edges + earliest arrival from one source ⇒ Dijkstra; the answer is the max shortest distance.

ds.answer: Adjacency List<List<int[]>> + PriorityQueue<int[]> {dist, node} + int[] dist
wrong: int[][] matrix with Floyd–Warshall for one source
ds.why: The heap always expands the closest unsettled node.

invariant.answer: When a node is popped with d == dist[node], d is its final shortest time.
wrong: Nodes are finalised in order of their number.
dist only decreases for the source.
Each node is pushed at most once.
invariant.why: Non-negative weights mean nothing popped later can improve it.

time.why: Each edge relaxation may push onto the heap.

wrong: BFS only works when n is small.

approach: Dijkstra from k. If any dist is still infinity return −1, else return the maximum dist.

twists.change: Every edge takes exactly one unit of time.
twists.statement: A signal starts at node k of a directed graph and every edge takes exactly one unit of time to cross. Return how long until all nodes receive it, or -1.
twists.trigger: every edge takes exactly one unit of time
twists.ds: ArrayDeque<Integer> BFS queue and int[] dist

nearMiss.why: Dijkstra still works, but with unit weights a FIFO queue already pops nodes in distance order: the heap is wasted.
The graph may have cycles; arrival time isn't a dependency order.
Edges are directed and you need times, not components.

twists.why: Unit weights ⇒ BFS levels are shortest times.
twists.approach: BFS from k; answer = max dist, or -1 if any node is unreached.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
statement: Given n cities and flights (from, to, price), return the cheapest price from src to dst using at most k stops (k + 1 flights), or −1 if no such route exists.

nearMiss.why: Always taking the cheapest next flight can use too many stops or miss a cheaper overall route.
Flights may form cycles, and ordering doesn't enforce the stop limit.
Connectivity doesn't give prices or count stops.

wrong: cheapest price from src to dst
trigger.why: Weighted shortest path with an edge-count limit ⇒ Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds (or Dijkstra/BFS over (city, stops) states).

ds.answer: int[] prices copied each round (Bellman-Ford) over the edge list
wrong: One int[] dist updated in place across rounds
PriorityQueue<int[]> by price only, without stops
ds.why: Copying the previous round prevents chaining several flights in one round (which would exceed k).

invariant.answer: After round r, prices[v] is the cheapest cost to reach v using at most r flights.
wrong: prices[v] is the cheapest cost with any number of flights.
Each round adds one city to the route.
invariant.why: So after k + 1 rounds, prices[dst] respects the stop limit.

time.why: k + 1 rounds over all flights.

wrong: Greedy needs the flights sorted by city number.

approach: prices = ∞ except src = 0. Repeat k + 1 times: tmp = copy; for each flight (u, v, p) if prices[u] + p < tmp[v] then tmp[v] = prices[u] + p; prices = tmp. Return prices[dst] or −1.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
statement: A grid of heights touches the Pacific on its top and left edges and the Atlantic on its bottom and right edges. Water flows to a neighbour of equal or lower height. Return every cell from which water can reach both oceans.

nearMiss.why: Flow can go up, down, left and right, so there's no acyclic order to fill a table in.
We only need reachability, not distances or costs.
Flow is directed (downhill only), and DSU only models undirected connectivity.

wrong: Water flows to a neighbour of equal or lower height
trigger.why: Searching from every cell is O((mn)²). Reverse it: flood uphill from each ocean's border and intersect the two reachable sets.

ds.answer: Two boolean[m][n] reachable grids, filled by DFS/BFS seeded from each ocean's border cells
wrong: int[][] dp of max height reachable
One boolean[][] visited reused for both oceans
ds.why: One set per ocean; the answer is their intersection.

invariant.answer: pacific[r][c] is true iff water from (r, c) can flow to the Pacific; the reverse search only steps to neighbours of equal or greater height.
wrong: Cells on the diagonal always reach both oceans.
A cell reaches an ocean iff it is higher than all neighbours.
Each cell is visited once in total across both searches.
invariant.why: Reversing edges turns 'can reach the ocean' into 'reachable from the ocean'.

time.why: Each cell is visited at most once per ocean.

space.why: Two visited grids plus the stack/queue.

wrong: DP would need the heights sorted.
DP would only find one ocean.

approach: DFS/BFS from all top/left cells into pac, from all bottom/right cells into atl, moving to neighbours with height ≥ current. Collect cells true in both.

title: Max Area of Island
statement: In a binary grid, an island is a group of 1s connected up, down, left or right. Return the area of the largest island, or 0 if there are none.

nearMiss.why: Islands can snake in any direction, so a top-left-to-bottom-right table can't add up their area.
We need each island's size separately, not distances from a set of sources.
No rotation/spiral/in-place trick; it's connected-component search.

trigger.answer: connected up, down, left or right
wrong: the area of the largest island
trigger.why: 4-directional connected components on a grid ⇒ flood fill from each unvisited 1, counting cells.

ds.answer: Recursive DFS (or ArrayDeque<int[]> BFS) that marks cells visited by setting them to 0
ds.why: Mutating the grid doubles as the visited set.

invariant.answer: Each flood fill visits exactly one island, every one of its cells once, and returns its size.
wrong: Each row contains at most one island.
Islands are visited in order of size.
A cell can belong to two islands.
invariant.why: Marked cells are never revisited.

time.why: Each cell is processed once.

wrong: DP would only find square islands.
DP needs the grid to be square.

approach: For each 1: area = dfs(r, c) where dfs sets the cell to 0 and returns 1 + dfs of four neighbours; track the max.

title: Surrounded Regions
statement: A board contains 'X' and 'O'. Capture every region of 'O's that is fully enclosed by 'X' (no cell of the region on the border) by flipping it to 'X'. Modify the board in place.

nearMiss.why: It is an in-place grid update, but the decision depends on connectivity to the border, which needs a search.
Whether a region touches the border can't be decided in one sweep direction.
BFS from all border 'O's does work, but distances don't matter; it's plain reachability (any traversal).

trigger.answer: no cell of the region on the border
trigger.why: Invert the question: flood from border 'O's to mark the safe ones, then flip everything else.

ds.answer: DFS/BFS from border 'O's marking them with a temporary character (e.g. '#')
wrong: int[][] dp of distances to the border
ds.why: The temporary mark acts as the visited set.

invariant.answer: After the border floods, every 'O' still unmarked can't reach the border, so it must be surrounded.
wrong: Every 'O' next to an 'X' is surrounded.
Regions are captured in order of size.
invariant.why: Final pass: 'O' → 'X', '#' → 'O'.

time.why: Each cell visited a constant number of times.

wrong: In-place matrix tricks can't read characters.
Matrix traversal only works on square boards.
Matrix problems can't modify the input.

approach: Flood from every border 'O', marking '#'. Then flip remaining 'O' to 'X' and '#' back to 'O'.

title: As Far from Land as Possible
statement: In an n × n grid of 0 (water) and 1 (land), find the water cell whose distance to the nearest land cell is as large as possible, and return that distance (Manhattan). Return -1 if there is no land or no water.

nearMiss.why: A BFS from each water cell is O((n²)²); starting from ALL land cells at once gives every distance in one pass.
Every step costs 1, so Dijkstra adds a log factor for nothing.
Binary-searching the distance with a feasibility check is possible but slower and more complex.

trigger.answer: distance to the nearest land cell
trigger.why: 'Distance to the nearest of many sources' for every cell ⇒ seed the BFS queue with all sources.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<int[]> seeded with every land cell; the grid (or int[][] dist) records distances
wrong: One BFS queue per water cell
ds.why: Two DP sweeps (top-left, bottom-right) also work as the alternate.

invariant.answer: Cells are dequeued in non-decreasing distance from the nearest land, so the first time a water cell is reached is its final distance.
wrong: Each land cell's BFS runs separately.
Distances decrease as the queue empties.
Water cells are only visited from their nearest land cell's BFS.
invariant.why: The last level reached is the answer.

time.why: Each cell enqueued once.

wrong: Graph BFS only works on trees.
A single-source BFS would need weighted edges.

approach: Queue all land; if none or all, return -1. BFS by levels, turning water to visited; return the number of levels − 1.

title: Shortest Bridge
statement: A binary grid contains exactly two islands (4-directionally connected 1s). Return the smallest number of 0s you must flip to 1 to connect the two islands.

nearMiss.why: Every flip costs 1, so BFS levels are already the shortest distances.
DSU can tell when the islands join if you add water cells, but in what order? BFS from one whole island answers 'how many' directly.
Paths between islands can wind in any direction.

wrong: smallest number of 0s you must flip
trigger.why: Find one island (DFS), then BFS outward from ALL its cells at once until you touch the other island.

ds.answer: DFS to collect island A into an ArrayDeque<int[]>, then level-by-level BFS from that queue
wrong: BFS from a single cell of island A
ds.why: Starting from one cell would overcount distances.

invariant.answer: After d BFS levels, the visited region is every cell within d flips of island A; the first time island B is touched, d is the answer.
wrong: Both islands grow at the same time.
The BFS starts from the island's centre.
Each level flips exactly one cell.
invariant.why: Multi-source BFS = distance to the nearest source cell.

time.why: Each cell visited a constant number of times.

wrong: Dijkstra would return the longest bridge.

approach: Find the first 1, DFS its island, marking 2 and enqueueing. BFS levels: on reaching a 1 return level; else mark water and enqueue.

title: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies
statement: Each recipe lists ingredients; an ingredient may itself be another recipe. You start with unlimited supplies of some basic items. Return every recipe you can eventually make.

nearMiss.why: A set of available items is part of it, but repeatedly scanning all recipes until nothing changes is O(n²); in-degrees schedule them directly.
Dependencies are directed: making A needs B, not the other way, so DSU's undirected groups don't fit.
There's no choice to try and undo; a recipe is makeable once all its ingredients are.

trigger.answer: an ingredient may itself be another recipe
wrong: every recipe you can eventually make
trigger.why: Items depend on other items ⇒ dependency graph; makeable = reached by Kahn's algorithm (cycles never reach in-degree 0).

ds.answer: HashMap<String, List<String>> ingredient → recipes, HashMap<String, Integer> in-degree, ArrayDeque<String> seeded with supplies
ds.why: In-degree = number of ingredients still missing.

invariant.answer: An item is dequeued only after all of its ingredients were dequeued, so every dequeued recipe is makeable; recipes in a cycle never reach in-degree 0.
wrong: Recipes are made in alphabetical order.
Every recipe is dequeued exactly once.
invariant.why: Kahn's algorithm naturally excludes cycles.

time.answer: O(R + I + S) for recipes, ingredient edges and supplies
time.why: Each edge processed once.

wrong: Hashing would give the recipes in the wrong order.
Hashing only works if there are no supplies.

approach: inDeg[recipe] = #ingredients; edges ingredient → recipe. Queue supplies. Pop item; for each dependent recipe: if −−inDeg == 0, add to answer and queue.

title: Minimum Height Trees
statement: Given an undirected tree with n nodes as an edge list, return all nodes that, if chosen as the root, give a tree of minimum height.

nearMiss.why: BFS from every node to measure height is O(n²); peeling leaves finds the centre in O(n).
Rerooting DP works but is more intricate; the input is a general tree as edges, not a rooted binary tree.
Edges are unweighted, and we want the centre, not one distance.

trigger.answer: give a tree of minimum height
wrong: an undirected tree with n nodes
trigger.why: Minimum height roots are the tree's centre (1 or 2 nodes) ⇒ peel leaves layer by layer, Kahn-style with degrees.

ds.answer: List<List<Integer>> adjacency, int[] degree, ArrayDeque<Integer> of current leaves
wrong: int[] height computed by BFS from each node
ds.why: Leaves are degree-1 nodes.

invariant.answer: After removing a layer of leaves, the remaining nodes form a tree with the same centre; stop when ≤ 2 nodes remain.
wrong: The centre is the node with the highest degree.
Each round removes exactly one node.
The answer is always a single node.
invariant.why: Trimming leaves shortens every longest path at both ends.

time.why: Each node and edge removed once.

wrong: Graph traversal can't be used on trees.
BFS would find the leaves, not the roots.

approach: If n ≤ 2 return all. Queue leaves. remaining = n. While remaining > 2: pop the whole leaf layer, decrement neighbours' degrees, queue new leaves. Return the queue.

title: Number of Provinces
statement: Given an n × n adjacency matrix where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means cities i and j are directly linked, return the number of groups of cities that are connected directly or indirectly.

nearMiss.why: Links are undirected and order doesn't matter; there are no dependencies.
The matrix is just an adjacency encoding; walking it spirally or in place has no meaning.
Only connectivity matters, not distances.

trigger.why: Count connected components of an undirected graph ⇒ union-find (or DFS from each unvisited city).

ds.answer: int[] parent with path compression and union by rank, plus a components counter
ds.why: Each successful union reduces the count by one.

invariant.answer: Two cities share a root iff the edges processed so far connect them; components = n − successful unions.
wrong: parent[i] is always i's direct neighbour.
Roots are always the smallest index.
invariant.why: Unions of already-connected cities don't change the count.

time.why: The matrix has n² entries; DSU operations are near-constant.

wrong: Topological sort only works on trees.
Topo sort would need the matrix sorted.

approach: count = n; for i < j with isConnected[i][j] == 1: if union(i, j) count−−. Return count.

title: Satisfiability of Equality Equations
statement: Each equation is a string like "a==b" or "a!=b" over single lowercase-letter variables. Return true if you can assign integers to the variables so that all equations hold.

nearMiss.why: Trying assignments is exponential; equality is transitive, so grouping is enough.
A map of direct equalities misses transitive ones (a==b, b==c ⇒ a==c).
Equalities are symmetric; there's no direction or ordering.

trigger.answer: assign integers to the variables so that all equations hold
trigger.why: == is an equivalence relation ⇒ union all equalities first, then any != inside one group is a contradiction.

ds.answer: int[26] parent (union-find over letters)
ds.why: 26 variables, tiny DSU.

invariant.answer: After processing all == equations, two variables share a root iff they must be equal; a != between same-root variables is unsatisfiable.
wrong: Each variable has at most one equal partner.
The order of equations changes the answer.
invariant.why: Two passes: all == first, then check !=.

time.why: Two passes over the equations.

wrong: Backtracking would need the equations sorted.

approach: Pass 1: union(x, y) for every "x==y". Pass 2: for every "x!=y", if find(x) == find(y) return false. Return true.

title: Path With Minimum Effort
statement: Walk from the top-left to the bottom-right cell of a height grid, moving in four directions. A route's effort is the largest absolute height difference between consecutive cells on it. Return the minimum effort.

nearMiss.why: Plain BFS counts steps; here edges have different costs and the path cost is a maximum, so you need a priority order.
Moves go in all four directions, so there's no acyclic fill order.
There's one source, and edges aren't unit-weight.

trigger.answer: the largest absolute height difference between consecutive cells
wrong: from the top-left to the bottom-right
trigger.why: Minimise the bottleneck of a path ⇒ Dijkstra with cost = max(cost so far, edge) (also: binary search the effort + BFS, or Kruskal-style DSU).

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<int[]> of {effort, r, c}, int[][] best filled with Integer.MAX_VALUE
wrong: int[][] dp filled row by row
ds.why: Dijkstra works because max(·) never decreases along a path.

invariant.answer: When a cell is polled with effort e, e is the minimum possible bottleneck to reach it.
wrong: Cells are polled in order of their height.
The first path found to the target is the shortest in steps.
invariant.why: Same proof as Dijkstra, with max instead of +.

time.why: Each cell may be pushed a few times.

wrong: BFS can't move in four directions.
BFS would need a sorted grid.
BFS gives the maximum effort instead.

approach: Dijkstra from (0, 0) with cost 0; relax neighbour with max(cost, |Δh|) if it improves best. Return when the target is polled.

title: Swim in Rising Water
statement: In an n × n grid, cell values are distinct elevations. At time t the water level is t and you can swim between adjacent cells whose elevations are both at most t. Return the least time at which you can get from the top-left to the bottom-right.

nearMiss.why: A BFS for a FIXED t is the check; finding the least t needs priority order (or a search over t).
You can swim in any direction, so there's no fill order.
The heap is ordering a frontier by path bottleneck, not selecting k items.

trigger.why: The time a path needs is its maximum elevation ⇒ minimise a path's bottleneck: Dijkstra with max (or binary search t + flood fill).

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<int[]> of {maxElevationSoFar, r, c} and boolean[][] visited
ds.why: Pop the reachable cell with the lowest elevation each time.

invariant.answer: The polled cell's key is the least water level at which it becomes reachable from the start.
wrong: Cells are polled row by row.
Time increases by 1 per cell visited.
The key is the number of steps taken.
invariant.why: Bottleneck Dijkstra.

time.why: n² cells through a heap.

wrong: BFS can't handle elevations above n.
BFS would give the most time.

approach: Heap from (grid[0][0], 0, 0). Poll; if target return key; mark visited; push unvisited neighbours with max(key, grid[nr][nc]).
